Comet Shoemaker-Levy 9. The first and only comet known to have impacted a planet in recorded history. Discovered in 1993 already fragmented into a string of pearls of more than 20 nuclei, it was captured into Jupiter's orbit and systematically struck the planet over six days in July 1994. The impacts produced explosion fireballs, scars visible for months, and seismic shocks, making it a watershed event in planetary science.

The comet was discovered on March 24th, 1993 by Carolyn Shoemaker, Eugene Shoemaker, and David Levy. It was already fragmented into a train of fragments when found. Jupiter's tidal forces — the Roche limit — had gravitationally shattered it during an earlier close approach. The 1992 encounter disrupted the nucleus into roughly 20 large pieces.

The comet was trapped in Jupiter's orbit after the 1992 pass. Calculations showed it was doomed to collide with Jupiter at perihelion two years later. The impacts occurred July 16th through 22nd, 1994. A train of fragments slammed into Jupiter's upper atmosphere in rapid succession, each explosion visible from Earth with modest telescopes. Some fireballs exceeded 10,000 kilometers across.

Dark scars persisted for weeks. The largest impacts created rings and clouds of heated gas, disrupting Jupiter's atmospheric belts and provoking seismic oscillations detected worldwide. The energies were enormous. The largest impacts released roughly 600 megatons of TNT equivalent, far exceeding the Tunguska event that flattened Siberia in 1908.

Jupiter's immense gravity was both the comet's captor and its executioner. Shoemaker-Levy 9 provided the only direct observation of planetary bombardment and redefined understanding of comet hazards and planetary impact processes. The comet's fragmentation exemplifies how differential gravity across an extended body can tear it apart.
